t: Watering Plants II — Two Pointers, Two Cans
o: **Understanding the problem.** Alice sweeps plants left-to-right and Bob right-to-left simultaneously; each must fully water the plant they reach, refilling first (instantly, counted) when short, and the lone meeting plant goes to whoever holds more water — Alice on ties. In `[2,2,3,3]` with capacity 5 each, Alice waters plants 0-1 while Bob refills once for plant 2 (needs 3, has 2): one refill total. With capacities 3 and 4 both walkers refill once (answer 2), and a single plant `[5]` is handled by Alice (10 >= 8) with zero refills. Constraints guarantee every capacity is at least `max(plants)`, so refill-then-water never fails, and n up to $10^5$ demands a linear sweep.
k: Apart from the meeting plant, Alice and Bob act independently — simulate both inward walks with two pointers.
Odd n leaves plant n/2 contested: compare leftover water (Alice wins ties) before charging a refill.
capacity >= max(plants) guarantees a single refill always enables watering.
Each pointer advances once per round, so the work is strictly O(n).

a.i: Track both cans' current contents. Each round Alice handles plants[l], Bob handles plants[r], refilling when short. When l == r (odd n), award that plant by comparing leftovers and charge the winner a refill if needed; for even n the pointers cross without meeting and the loop simply ends.
s: Initialize a = capacityA, b = capacityB, l = 0, r = n-1, refills = 0.
While l < r: refill a if a < plants[l], then a -= plants[l], l++; refill b if b < plants[r], then b -= plants[r], r--.
If l == r after the loop: take the larger can (Alice on ties); add 1 refill if it cannot cover plants[l].
a.t: O(n) — every plant is handled exactly once.
a.sp: O(1) — two can variables and counters.

a.i: Alice's route before the middle is a fixed prefix and Bob's a fixed suffix; each walker's refill count is just the greedy segmentation of their segment into capacity-sized chunks, with leftover equal to capacity minus the last unfinished chunk. Compute (refills, leftover) per segment, then settle the middle plant (odd n) by comparing leftovers. Same complexity as the direct simulation but a cleaner per-person mental model.
s: Let m = floor(n/2); Alice segment covers indices 0..m-1, Bob segment covers n-1 down to m+1 (odd n) or m (even n).
Greedy-sweep each segment: refill whenever the can cannot cover the next plant; record refills and leftover.
Odd n: winner has the larger leftover (Alice wins ties); add 1 refill if the winner's leftover < plants[m].
Return Alice refills + Bob refills + middle penalty.
a.t: O(n) — each of the two segments scanned once.

w: Write Approach 1 first and validate it against example 3 (single plant, Alice waters because 10 > 8). Pitfalls: watering the middle plant twice or not at all (the l == r case fires exactly once, only for odd n); forgetting that Alice wins ties; assuming Bob's leftover decides when Alice already has more. Follow-ups: Watering Plants I (one walker, same refill logic), or reporting where the last refill happened — both reuse this simulation.
